An ebook loan is already conditional (it expires automatically), and libraries accept limits (one user per licensed copy, for example) that imitate physical circulation. Those conditions explain ordinary returns. They don't explain why a publisher can reach into an active loan and revoke it. The card catalog can change tomorrow; it shouldn't erase the book already open on the desk.

There may be legitimate reasons to withdraw a title—an accidental release, a rights dispute, or a serious file defect—but those reasons do not make silent mid-loan deletion fair. Publishers and ebook vendors should disclose withdrawal rules, notify libraries before action, and preserve access through the original due date. structured_output.draft:
No. Returning a library ebook at the end of a loan means the agreed borrowing period expired. A publisher withdrawing the title during that period is different: the lender and reader followed the rules, but access disappeared anyway. The file may be digital, yet the broken promise is perfectly concrete—reading stops in midchapter.

An ebook loan is already conditional (it expires automatically), and libraries accept limits (one user per licensed copy, for example) that imitate physical circulation. Those conditions explain ordinary returns. They don't explain why a publisher can reach into an active loan and revoke it. The card catalog can change tomorrow; it shouldn't erase the book already open on the desk.

There may be legitimate reasons to withdraw a title—an accidental release, a rights dispute, or a serious file defect—but those reasons do not make silent mid-loan deletion fair. A library can stop new checkouts (a prospective change) while preserving existing loans (a limited transition). That approach respects both the publisher’s problem and the reader’s reliance.

That distinction matters because public-library lending isn't a private favor from a platform. It is a public service delivered through contracts. Readers depend on the loan period, just as libraries depend on licenses being honored.

We should insist on a simple standard: withdrawal may block future loans, but it must not terminate an active one except when keeping the file available would itself be unlawful or unsafe. Publishers and ebook vendors should disclose withdrawal rules, notify libraries before action, and preserve access through the original due date. Libraries should demand those protections in their contracts and explain exceptions plainly.

So this wasn't the digital equivalent of returning a book. It was closer to the publisher taking the book back before it was due. The format changed; the obligation didn't.
